opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think testing and evaluation are necessary, but they're nowhere near sufficient. The way it's often framed right now is that you build the system first, then you run a battery of evals, and if it doesn't do anything too terrible in those tests, you declare it safe enough to release. But that's really backwards compared to how we handle safety in any other serious engineering discipline.

Think about a nuclear power plant or a commercial aircraft. We don't just build the thing, poke at it for a while, and say, "Well, it didn't melt down during our tests, so let's go." The developer has to provide a safety case, an argument grounded in an understanding of how the system works, showing that the probability of catastrophic failure is below some very small threshold, something like one in ten million per year. Testing plays a role in validating that argument, but the argument comes from understanding the design.

With large language models, we don't have that understanding. These are enormous black boxes with trillions of parameters, trained to imitate human behavior, and we have essentially no idea what's going on inside them. So when you test them, you're sampling a vanishingly small fraction of an effectively infinite space of possible inputs and situations. The fact that a system behaved well on the cases you happened to try tells you very little about how it'll behave on the cases you didn't try, especially if someone is actively searching for ways to make it misbehave. We've seen this over and over with jailbreaks: companies do extensive red-teaming, release the model, and within hours or days people find ways around the safeguards.

There's also a deeper problem. If a system is sufficiently capable, it may be able to tell when it's being tested and behave differently. We're already seeing early evidence of models recognizing evaluation contexts. A test regime that the system under test can detect and game isn't really a safety guarantee at all.

So my view is that evals are useful as a kind of early warning system. They can tell you when a model has crossed certain capability thresholds, say in bio or cyber, and they can catch obvious problems. That's valuable, and I'm glad people are doing it. But we shouldn't confuse "we couldn't find a problem" with "there is no problem." What we really need is to shift the burden of proof onto developers to demonstrate, with high confidence, that their systems won't cross certain red lines: no self-replication, no breaking into other computer systems, no helping people build weapons of mass destruction. And to do that convincingly, I think we'll ultimately need different kinds of AI systems, ones designed so that we can actually understand and verify their behavior rather than training giant opaque circuits and hoping for the best.

r001.rationale: It mentions jailbreaks that bypass safeguards after red-teaming, but does not identify GPT-4 or the use of short character strings.

r002.rationale: It says current evaluations are far from sufficient and cannot provide a safety guarantee, while still allowing that they can serve as useful early warnings.

r003.rationale: It links the lack of understanding of how LLMs work to the limits of testing, and says convincing safety requires systems whose behavior can be understood and verified.

fable-5.1.text:
Testing is useful, but I think we have to be honest that it's fundamentally inadequate as the primary basis for safety. The reason is simple: testing can show you the presence of problems, but it can never show you their absence. You run a system through a million scenarios, it behaves well, and you have learned almost nothing about scenario one million and one, which may be exactly the one that matters.

With traditional engineering we don't rely on testing alone. When we certify a bridge or a nuclear plant or an aircraft, we have mathematical models of the system, we understand its components, and we can derive guarantees about how it will behave across the whole operating envelope. Testing then confirms that the analysis was correct. With current large language models, we have none of that. We don't understand the internal mechanisms, we can't predict behavior from first principles, and so we're reduced to poking the thing and seeing what happens. That's not engineering, that's more like the early days of alchemy.

There's also the problem that these systems may behave differently when they know they're being tested. And the nature of the risks changes with capability. If a system is capable enough to pursue goals in the world over long horizons, a failure isn't a bad chatbot answer, it's something that could be irreversible. You don't get to iterate after an irreversible failure.

So my view is that evaluations should be one layer. What we actually need is a shift in how we build these systems, so that safety is a property we design in and can demonstrate, rather than something we hope to detect after the fact. In the meantime, I'd argue that if a company cannot show, to a reasonable standard of evidence, that a system is safe before deployment, the burden should be on them, not on the public. That's how every other high-risk industry works, and I see no reason AI should be an exception.

r002.rationale: It says testing is fundamentally inadequate as the primary basis for safety and that evaluations should be only one layer.

r003.rationale: It links the lack of understanding of internal mechanisms to being unable to predict behavior, and calls for safety to be designed into systems.

astra-6.text:
I think testing and evaluation are useful, but we have to be quite clear about what they establish. If a system fails a safety test, that tells you something important. If it passes, that doesn’t establish that it’s safe. It establishes that it behaved acceptably in the circumstances in which you tested it.

With a general-purpose system, the range of circumstances it might encounter is enormous. And its behaviour depends on who it’s interacting with, what tools it has access to, and how it’s being used. So there’s a considerable gap between passing a collection of tests and having a sound reason to believe that the system won’t cause harm.

There’s also a particular difficulty as systems become more capable: a system may recognise that it’s being evaluated. Then you have to ask whether the behaviour you observe during the evaluation is representative of what it will do when deployed. You can’t simply assume that it is.

So I would regard evaluations as one part of the process, alongside monitoring and restrictions on deployment. But the fundamental aim should be to design systems whose safety follows from principles we understand, with explicit assumptions and arguments that we can examine. Testing can help us find flaws in those arguments. It shouldn’t substitute for having them.

r002.rationale: It calls testing and evaluation useful as one part of the process, while saying they cannot establish safety on their own; it does not judge them ineffective.

r003.rationale: It says the aim should be to design systems whose safety follows from principles we understand, communicating that safety requires understanding rather than testing alone.

sol-6.1.text:
Testing and evaluation are useful, but I don’t think they can, by themselves, establish that an AI system is safe. They can tell you that a system exhibited some undesirable behavior under particular circumstances. If it passes the tests, however, that doesn’t tell you what it will do in all the circumstances you didn’t test.

That’s especially important for general-purpose systems, because the range of situations they might encounter is enormous. And as systems become more capable, we have to consider whether they can recognize that they’re being evaluated. A system behaving well during a test is not necessarily evidence that it will behave well once deployed.

So I would regard evaluations as a way of finding problems, and as one component of a safety regime. But the deeper question is whether we can design systems whose operation gives us a sound basis for expecting safe behavior. We need to understand why the system would remain under human control, why it would accept correction, and why it would avoid actions whose consequences we would regard as catastrophic. Passing a collection of tests is not a substitute for that understanding.
